newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Papua New Guinea's Chan reclaims prime ministership.
newsitem.headline: Papua New Guinea's Chan reclaims prime ministership.

text.p: Papua New Guinea sank into political confusion on Monday after two politicians declared themselves to be the country's prime minister.

Former prime minister Sir Julius Chan, who stood down at the height of a political crisis in March, said he had resumed the office after the completion of an inquiry into the government's abortive plan to use mercenaries to quell an island rebellion.
"I have at noon today (Monday) resumed the full duties and responsibilities of Prime Minister of Papua New Guinea," Chan said in a statement.
His announcement at a news conference, less than two weeks ahead of national elections, came only one hour after caretaker prime minister John Giheno declared he would stay on in office.
"My appointment is legally binding and the perogative is mine to vacate the office," Giheno told reporters.

Chan stood aside in March pending the inquiry's outcome after mutinous troops blockaded parliament in protest over the hiring of overseas mercenaries to quell a protracted seccessionist revolt on Bougainville island.
The 10-day army revolt sparked Papua New Guinea's most serious political crisis since the country gained independence 22 years ago as thousands of protesters took to the streets.
An inquiry subsequently investigated Chan's role in the awarding of a US$36 million contract to the Sandline International mercenary group.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Chan, releasing the 125-page final report into the Sandline contract, said the inquiry had cleared him of any wrongdoing.
"Now I have been cleared, it is right that I assume the prime ministership again," Chan said.

"All the advice I have received is that this has been the Commission's finding in regard to myself, and accordingly there is no impediment, legal or otherwise, acting against my resumption," Chan said.
However, Giheno said he had no plan to leave office and he called for an inquiry into how the Sandline report was released to "unauthorised persons".
"I will stay in office if it means preventing the country from facing a similar crisis it experienced at the height of the Sandline fiasco," Giheno said.
Chan told reporters that evidence already given to the inquiry showed that he had been cleared of any allegations of corruption surrounding the contract.
"It's been completed and all of us have been exonerated," he said. He said Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta and Defence Minister Mathias Ijape would also resume office immediately.

The inquiry into the Sandline contract, conducted by Judge Warwick Andrew, followed an army revolt led by the army leader, Brigadier General Jerry Singirok who was sacked for refusing to cooperate with the mercenaries.
Papua New Guinea elections are due to start on June 14 with voting expected to take about three weeks to complete.
